'''Jeffrey H. Shapiro''' is a [[Julius A. Stratton]] Professor of [[electrical engineering and computer science]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and the former director of the [[Research Laboratory of Electronics|Research Laboratory of Electronics.]]<ref>[http://www.rle.mit.edu/shapiro Jeffrey Shapiro]</ref> He made seminal contributions to understanding the fundamental quantum limits on [[communications]], generation, detection, and application of quantum [[squeezed state]], [[ghost imaging]], and [[quantum information science]].  He invented the microchannel-plate spatial light modulator with [[Cardinal Warde]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Kalb|first=Gilbert|title=Massively Parallel, Optical, and Neural Computing in the United States|year=1992|publisher=IOS Press|page=91|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7Ao4TBf4uv4C&pg=PA91 |author2=Robert Moxley|isbn=978-90-5199-097-3}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Shapiro received his S.B., S.M., E.E., and Ph.D. degrees in electrical engineering from MIT in 1967, 1968, 1969, and 1970, respectively. From 1970 to 1973, he was on the faculty of [[Case Western Reserve University]]. From 1973 to 1985, he was an associate professor of electrical engineering at MIT, and in 1985, he was promoted to professor of electrical engineering. He became a Julius A. Stratton Professor in 1999.

From 1989 to 1999, Shapiro served as the associate department head of MIT's department of electrical engineering and computer science. He was appointed director of the Research Laboratory of Electronics in 2001.<ref>[http://www.rle.mit.edu/rle-professor-jeffrey-h-shapiro-julius-a-stratton-professor-of-electrical-engineering-named-the-seventh-director-of-the-research-laboratory-of-electronics/ Shapiro appointed the seventh Director of RLE]</ref> He is also a director of MIT's Optical and Quantum Communications Group.<ref>{{cite web|last=Hardesty|first=Larry|title=Making quantum encryption practical|url=http://phys.org/news/2013-05-quantum-encryption.html|work=Phys.org|access-date=20 November 2013|date=May 21, 2013}}</ref>

== Research ==
Shapiro's research focuses on utilizing [[quantum mechanics|quantum mechanical effects]] to develop [[quantum metrology|metrology]] tools and applications, whose performance greatly exceeds what can be realized with conventional, [[classical physics|classical-physics]] systems. In particular, his group investigated the quantum limits on [[optical communications]], such as [[remote viewing]], and derived the [[quantum capacity|capacity]] of quantum channels. His group also demonstrated high-performance [[quantum entanglement|entanglement]] sources and took advantage of these sources to implement [[quantum key distribution]] systems. Shapiro's group pioneered in developing [[quantum illumination]],<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Zhang | first1=Zheshen | last2=Tengner | first2=Maria | last3=Zhong | first3=Tian | last4=Wong | first4=Franco N. C. | last5=Shapiro | first5=Jeffrey H. | title=Entanglement's Benefit Survives an Entanglement-Breaking Channel | journal=Physical Review Letters | publisher=American Physical Society (APS) | volume=111 | issue=1 | date=2013-07-01 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.111.010501 | article-number=010501| pmid=23862986 | arxiv=1303.5343 | bibcode=2013PhRvL.111a0501Z | doi-access=free }}</ref> which enables use of entanglement in lossy and noisy environments.<ref>{{cite journal | title=Broken quantum links still work | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=499 | issue=7457 | year=2013 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/499129a | page=129| doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>''Fragility of entanglement no bar to quantum secrets'', [[New Scientist]] July 17, 2013([https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn23882-fragility-of-entanglement-no-bar-to-quantum-secrets.html#.Uo15S5GzweY])</ref>
